current_example.problem: Express $\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm d x$ as the limit of a right Riemann sum.
current_example.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k)\cdot\Delta x,
$$

where $x_k = a + k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x =  \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm d x,
$$

the function is $f(x) = x^2,$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{2-1}{n} = \dfrac 1 n.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\,Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{k}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[{(1+\frac{k}{n})}^{2}\,\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$
